q: What was the real birth name of the British novelist and essayist George Orwell (1903–1950)?
e: George Orwell was born Eric Arthur Blair on 25 June 1903 in Motihari, Bihar (then Bengal Presidency, British India). He adopted the pen name 'George Orwell' in 1933 for 'Down and Out in Paris and London', taking 'George' from England's patron saint and 'Orwell' from the River Orwell in Suffolk.

q: In which town of present-day Bihar, India, was George Orwell born while his father worked in the Opium Department of the Indian Civil Service?
e: Eric Arthur Blair was born in Motihari (East Champaran district, Bihar) in 1903, where his father Richard Walmesley Blair served as a sub-deputy opium agent. His birthplace in Motihari has been preserved as a heritage site.

q: Before becoming a full-time writer, Orwell served from 1922 to 1927 as an officer in the Indian Imperial Police in which British colony?
e: After leaving Eton College in 1921, Orwell joined the Indian Imperial Police in Burma (1922–1927). His deep disillusionment with British imperialism directly inspired his novel 'Burmese Days' (1934) and essays 'A Hanging' (1931) and 'Shooting an Elephant' (1936).

q: In which year was George Orwell's famous political allegory 'Animal Farm' first published?
e: 'Animal Farm' (originally subtitled 'A Fairy Story') was published in August 1945 by Secker & Warburg after several publishers rejected it during WWII out of sensitivity toward the Soviet Union. It satirizes the 1917 Russian Revolution and its Stalinist betrayal.

q: In 'Animal Farm', which wise old Middle White boar inspires the animals' rebellion with his dream and the revolutionary song 'Beasts of England'?
e: Old Major represents Karl Marx (and Vladimir Lenin), articulating the principles of 'Animalism' before dying three nights after his speech. Napoleon and Snowball subsequently lead the rebellion against the drunken farmer Mr. Jones.

q: Which hardworking cart-horse in 'Animal Farm' lives by the two personal maxims "I will work harder" and "Napoleon is always right"?
e: Boxer symbolizes the loyal, exploited Soviet working class (proletariat) whose immense physical strength builds the windmill. Once he collapses from overwork, Napoleon callously sells him to the knacker (horse slaughterer) to buy whisky.

q: In 'Animal Farm', the original Seven Commandments of Animalism are finally erased and replaced by which single altered commandment on the barn wall?
o: "No animal shall drink alcohol to excess."
"All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others."
"Man is the only creature that consumes without producing."
e: The paradox "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others" is the climax of the pigs' linguistic and ideological corruption in Chapter 10, exposing how totalitarian elites subvert egalitarian revolutions.

q: Who is the protagonist of George Orwell's dystopian masterpiece 'Nineteen Eighty-Four' (1949), working as a clerk in the Records Department of the Ministry of Truth?
e: Winston Smith (aged 39, living in Victory Mansions in Airstrip One, Oceania) is an Outer Party member whose job is to falsify historical records at the Ministry of Truth. His quiet rebellion through a secret diary and love affair with Julia drives the plot.

q: Which of the following is the official three-part slogan of the Party (Ingsoc) emblazoned on the white pyramid of the Ministry of Truth in 'Nineteen Eighty-Four'?
o: "War is Peace, Freedom is Slavery, Ignorance is Strength"
"Truth is Power, Memory is Crime, Silence is Safety"
e: The three paradoxical Party slogans — "War is Peace / Freedom is Slavery / Ignorance is Strength" — embody the core mechanism of 'Doublethink' in Oceania's totalitarian state under Big Brother.

q: In 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', what is the simplified, shrinking official language engineered by the Party to eliminate the very range of rebellious thought?
e: Newspeak (detailed in the novel's Appendix, 'The Principles of Newspeak') systematically eliminates synonyms, antonyms, and nuanced vocabulary so that 'Thoughtcrime' (crimethink) becomes literally impossible to express.

q: What is the name of the dreaded torture chamber inside the Ministry of Love in 'Nineteen Eighty-Four' that contains "the worst thing in the world" for each prisoner?
e: In Room 101, O'Brien breaks Winston's last remnant of loyalty to Julia by confronting him with his deepest phobia (a cage of starving rats), forcing him to cry "Do it to Julia!". Orwell named it after a dreary BBC conference room (Room 101) where he attended tedious meetings.

q: Which 1933 autobiographical work was George Orwell's FIRST full-length published book, chronicling his experiences of poverty as a dishwasher (plongeur) and tramp?
o: Down and Out in Paris and London
e: 'Down and Out in Paris and London' (published January 1933 by Victor Gollancz) was Orwell's debut book and the first to bear the pseudonym 'George Orwell'. It exposed urban destitution, lodging houses, and spike (casual ward) conditions.

q: Which 1938 personal account documents George Orwell's firsthand combat experiences fighting for the Republican POUM militia in the Spanish Civil War?
e: 'Homage to Catalonia' (1938) recounts Orwell's service on the Aragon front (where he was shot through the throat) and the May Days of 1937 in Barcelona, when Soviet-backed Communists suppressed the anti-Stalinist POUM — turning Orwell into a lifelong opponent of Stalinism.

q: In Orwell's famous 1936 essay 'Shooting an Elephant', where is the narrator stationed as a sub-divisional police officer pressured by a crowd of two thousand locals to shoot a straying elephant?
e: Set in Moulmein (Lower Burma) and published in 'New Writing' (1936), 'Shooting an Elephant' uses the killing of a calm working elephant to reveal the central irony of imperialism: "when the white man turns tyrant it is his own freedom that he destroys."

q: Which 1934 debut novel by George Orwell is set in the fictional Burmese town of Kyauktada and centres on the disillusioned timber merchant John Flory?
e: 'Burmese Days' (1934, first published in the USA due to British libel fears) critiques colonial racism, the exclusiveness of the European Club, and bureaucratic corruption through John Flory, Dr. Veraswami, and the scheming magistrate U Po Kyin.

q: During World War II (1941–1943), Orwell worked as a Talks Producer broadcasting literary and anti-fascist programmes to India for which organization before becoming literary editor of the left-wing weekly 'Tribune'?
e: Orwell worked for the BBC Eastern Service (1941–1943), collaborating with figures like Mulk Raj Anand and T.S. Eliot; his wartime broadcasting frustration inspired the Ministry of Truth in 'Nineteen Eighty-Four'. He later served as literary editor of 'Tribune' (1943–1945), writing his 'As I Please' column.

q: On which remote Scottish island did George Orwell rent the isolated farmhouse 'Barnhill' (1946–1949) to write 'Nineteen Eighty-Four' while battling severe tuberculosis?
e: Orwell lived at Barnhill on the remote Isle of Jura (Inner Hebrides, Scotland) from 1946 to 1949, completing 'Nineteen Eighty-Four' despite worsening tuberculosis. He died in London on 21 January 1950 at age 46.

q:
Match List-I (Character in 'Animal Farm') with List-II (Historical Allegorical Parallel):
List-I:
1. Napoleon
2. Snowball
3. Squealer
4. Mr. Jones
List-II:
(a) Leon Trotsky
(b) Tsar Nicholas II
(c) Joseph Stalin
(d) Soviet Propaganda / Pravda
e: In 'Animal Farm' (1945): Napoleon = Joseph Stalin; Snowball = Leon Trotsky (brilliant strategist expelled by Napoleon's nine ferocious dogs, symbolizing the NKVD/secret police); Squealer = Soviet propaganda/Pravda; Mr. Jones = Tsar Nicholas II.

q: What does the tame raven 'Moses' symbolize in 'Animal Farm' with his constant tales of 'Sugarcandy Mountain' in the sky?
o: The Russian Orthodox Church and organized religion promising an afterlife reward
e: Moses represents the Russian Orthodox Church — initially expelled after the revolution, he is later tolerated and given a daily gill of beer by Napoleon because his promise of 'Sugarcandy Mountain' keeps the overworked animals docile (echoing Marx's "opium of the people").

q: Which cynical, long-lived donkey in 'Animal Farm' refuses to take sides in farm politics, famously remarking "Donkeys live a long time. None of you has ever seen a dead donkey"?
e: Benjamin is the oldest, most skeptical animal on the farm who can read as well as any pig yet chooses passivity, representing cynical intellectuals who see through totalitarian deceit too late to stop it (he only reacts passionately when Boxer is taken to the knacker).

q: In 'Animal Farm', which neighbouring human farmer of Pinchfield Farm represents Adolf Hitler (Nazi Germany), who pays Napoleon with forged banknotes for timber before attacking the farm in the Battle of the Windmill?
e: Mr. Frederick (Pinchfield) allegorizes Nazi Germany/Hitler (the forged-banknote timber deal parallels the 1939 Nazi–Soviet Pact, followed by the 1941 German invasion = Battle of the Windmill). Mr. Pilkington (Foxwood) represents Britain/Allies; Mr. Whymper is the solicitor intermediary.

q: At the chilling final scene of 'Animal Farm', why can the animals peering through the farmhouse window no longer tell the pigs from the humans?
o: Because Mr. Jones returns and paints all the pigs white
Because Snowball returns and signs a treaty with Pilkington
Because all the pigs leave the farm for England
Because the pigs walk on two legs, wear clothes, play cards with human farmers, and restore the name 'Manor Farm'
e: In Chapter 10, Napoleon announces the farm's name is restored to 'Manor Farm' and plays cards with Mr. Pilkington (both simultaneously playing an Ace of Spades — foreshadowing the Cold War). Looking from pig to man and man to pig, the animals find it "impossible to say which was which."

q:
Match List-I (Ministry in Oceania) with List-II (Its Ironic Actual Function in 'Nineteen Eighty-Four'):
List-I:
1. Ministry of Truth (Minitrue)
2. Ministry of Peace (Minipax)
3. Ministry of Love (Miniluv)
4. Ministry of Plenty (Miniplenty)
List-II:
(a) Economic rationing and perpetuating scarcity
(b) Law, order, surveillance, and torture
(c) Perpetual warfare
(d) Propaganda, censorship, and falsifying history
e: Oceania's four ministries embody Newspeak irony: Minitrue = propaganda & lies; Minipax = continuous war; Miniluv = windowless fortress of terror & torture (containing Room 101); Miniplenty = starvation & economic rationing.

q: In 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', who is the mysterious Inner Party official whom Winston mistakenly believes to be a secret member of the underground Brotherhood, only to discover he is Winston's ruthless interrogator and torturer?
e: O'Brien lures Winston and Julia into swearing allegiance to the Brotherhood and lends Winston 'The Theory and Practice of Oligarchical Collectivism', before personally supervising Winston's brutal re-education in the Ministry of Love. Mr. Charrington (the junk-shop owner) is also revealed to be a Thought Police agent.

q: What is 'Doublethink' as defined in George Orwell's 'Nineteen Eighty-Four'?
o: Speaking two European languages fluently in Oceania
Writing a diary entry in two different notebooks
Reporting a neighbour twice to the Thought Police
The mental power of holding two contradictory beliefs in one's mind simultaneously and accepting both of them
e: Doublethink is the psychological cornerstone of Ingsoc — simultaneously knowing and not knowing, forgetting inconvenient facts and recalling them when needed, exemplified by forcing Winston to genuinely see five fingers when O'Brien holds up four ("2 + 2 = 5").

q: In 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', who is the Party's chief ideological enemy and alleged leader of the underground 'Brotherhood', whose face appears daily during the 'Two Minutes Hate' (paralleling Leon Trotsky)?
e: Emmanuel Goldstein (a former leading Party figure turned arch-traitor, modelled on Leon Trotsky) is the scapegoat target of the daily 'Two Minutes Hate' and supposed author of the forbidden 'Book'. (Comrade Ogilvy is a fictional war hero invented by Winston at the Ministry of Truth.)

q: Which three rival totalitarian superstates divide the entire world in perpetual shifting warfare in 'Nineteen Eighty-Four'?
e: The world of 1984 is locked in eternal war among three superstates — Oceania (where Britain is 'Airstrip One'), Eurasia, and Eastasia — constantly switching alliances while rewriting history so that "Oceania has always been at war with Eastasia/Eurasia."

q: Which 1936 novel by George Orwell follows the struggling poet and bookshop assistant Gordon Comstock, who wages a futile war against the "money-god" symbolized by a despised potted houseplant?
e: 'Keep the Aspidistra Flying' (1936) portrays Gordon Comstock's bitter rebellion against middle-class commercialism and the aspidistra (a Victorian symbol of suburban respectability), until Rosemary's pregnancy compels him to accept bourgeois life and buy an aspidistra.

q: In George Orwell's 1939 novel 'Coming Up for Air', which middle-aged insurance salesman returns to his childhood Oxfordshire village of Lower Binfield in search of pre-WWI peace, only to find it transformed by modern commercialism and the looming shadow of WWII?
e: 'Coming Up for Air' (June 1939) uses George Bowling's nostalgic trip to Lower Binfield to capture Britain's pre-war anxiety, industrialization, and the death of rural pastoral innocence just before World War II.

q: Which 1935 experimental novel by Orwell traces the amnesia-stricken journey of Dorothy Hare — from her strict rector father's parish through hop-picking in Kent, homelessness in Trafalgar Square, and a dreary private school?
o: Down and Out in Paris and London
e: 'A Clergyman's Daughter' (1935) reflects James Joyce's experimental influence (notably the dramatic Trafalgar Square homeless scene) while exposing rural poverty, exploitative private schools (Ringwood House), and religious doubt.

q: Commissioned by Victor Gollancz's Left Book Club, which 1937 sociological work by Orwell investigates the grim living conditions of unemployed coal miners in Northern England in Part I before critiquing middle-class socialist intellectuals in Part II?
e: 'The Road to Wigan Pier' (1937) combines vivid investigative journalism of Lancashire/Yorkshire coal miners (Part I) with a blunt critique of class snobbery among British socialists (Part II), prompting Victor Gollancz to add a nervous foreword.

q: Published in 1931 in 'The Adelphi', Orwell's harrowing essay 'A Hanging' crystallizes his horror at capital punishment when the condemned Burmese prisoner does what unexpected small act on the walk to the gallows?
o: Steps slightly aside to avoid a puddle on the path
Hands his ring to the superintendent
Refuses to walk and sits down
e: Seeing the bound prisoner instinctively sidestep a puddle triggers Orwell's epiphany about "the unspeakable wrongness, of cutting a life short when it is in full tide" — a classic example of Orwell's concrete observational prose.

q: In his landmark 1946 essay 'Politics and the English Language', what central thesis does George Orwell advance about the connection between political decay and sloppy language?
o: Political corruption is completely unrelated to how people write.

Sloppy, pretentious, and euphemistic language corrupts clear thought and is deliberately used to defend the indefensible ("Political language is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable").
Writers should adopt more Latinate jargon and passive voice to appear objective.
English should be replaced by Esperanto to end war.
e: Published in 'Horizon' (April 1946), 'Politics and the English Language' identifies four vices (dying metaphors, operators/verbal false limbs, pretentious diction, meaningless words) and gives six famous rules for plain, honest prose.

q: In his 1946 autobiographical essay 'Why I Write', Orwell lists four great motives for writing prose — Sheer Egoism, Aesthetic Enthusiasm, Historical Impulse, and which fourth motive that dominated his work after 1936?
e: In 'Why I Write' (1946), Orwell famously declared: "Every line of serious work that I have written since 1936 has been written, directly or indirectly, against totalitarianism and for democratic socialism, as I understand it."

q: In his balanced 1949 essay 'Reflections on Gandhi' (published in 'Partisan Review'), what famous opening aphorism does Orwell coin regarding moral perfectionism?
o: "Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely."
"Saints should always be judged guilty until they are proved innocent."
e: In 'Reflections on Gandhi' (1949), Orwell opens with "Saints should always be judged guilty until they are proved innocent," yet concludes with warm admiration for Gandhi's courage, honesty, and anti-imperialism, noting how "clean a smell he has managed to leave behind."

q: In 'Animal Farm', which character is the ONLY animal who notices the night-time alteration of the Commandments on the barn wall (when Squealer falls off a ladder with a paintbrush) yet still fails to connect it to the pigs' betrayal, while Muriel the goat reads the altered text aloud?
e: When Squealer tumbles from the ladder at midnight with a lantern and white paint after altering the Fifth Commandment ("No animal shall drink alcohol — to excess"), the dogs escort him away; only old Benjamin "nodded his muzzle with a knowing air" and seemed to understand, yet said nothing, while Muriel later reads the altered wording to Clover.

q: What is the name of the sycophantic poet-pig in 'Animal Farm' who replaces 'Beasts of England' with the propaganda anthem "Animal Farm, Animal Farm, Never through me shalt thou come to harm" and composes the ode 'Comrade Napoleon'?
e: Minimus represents state-controlled Soviet artists/poets (like Maxim Gorky/Socialist Realist propagandists) who glorify Stalin. Pinkeye is the young pig who acts as Napoleon's food taster against poisoning.

q: In 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', what is the exact chilling opening sentence of Part One, Chapter 1, that immediately establishes the uncanny, off-kilter totalitarian atmosphere?
o: "Big Brother is watching you from every corner of London."
"It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen."
"All animals are equal, though winter had come early to Oceania."
"Winston Smith stepped out of the Ministry of Truth into the grey fog."
e: "It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen" immediately blends mundane British weather with the jarring 24-hour military clock ("thirteen"), signalling an alienated, militarized dystopia.

q: In 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', what is the significance of the grammatical tense used in the Appendix titled 'The Principles of Newspeak'?
o: It is written in future tense, showing Newspeak will triumph by 2050.
It is written in the PAST TENSE ("Newspeak was the official language of Oceania"), subtly implying that Big Brother's regime eventually collapsed in the future.
It is written entirely in Newspeak without Standard English.
It is narrated by O'Brien from Room 101.
e: Critics (like Margaret Atwood) highlight that the Appendix is written in the past tense from a post-totalitarian scholarly perspective ("Newspeak was..."), offering a quiet structural ray of hope despite Winston's personal defeat ("He loved Big Brother").

q: Which colleague of Winston Smith at the Ministry of Truth — a philologist compiling the Eleventh Edition of the Newspeak Dictionary — does Winston accurately predict will be "vaporized" (become an 'unperson') because he is "too intelligent" and "sees too clearly"?
e: Syme enthusiastically explains how Newspeak shrinks vocabulary ("It's a beautiful thing, the destruction of words"), yet his sharp intellect dooms him to be erased ('vaporized'). Ampleforth is arrested for leaving the word 'God' in a Kipling poem; Parsons is denounced by his own daughter for saying "Down with Big Brother" in his sleep.

q: Which earlier Russian dystopian novel (1921, published in English 1924) did Orwell review in 'Tribune' (1946) and acknowledge as a major structural influence on 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', preferring it over Aldous Huxley's 'Brave New World'?
e: Orwell admired Yevgeny Zamyatin's 'We' (1921, featuring the One State, Benefactor, glass walls, and a rebellious mathematician D-503) for grasping "the intuitive irrationality of totalitarianism" better than Huxley's 'Brave New World' (1932). Arthur Koestler's 'Darkness at Noon' (1940) also influenced Orwell's understanding of Moscow Show Trials.

q: In 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', which recurring nursery rhyme about London churches ("Oranges and lemons, say the bells of St. Clement's...") hauntingly culminates in the line "Here comes a candle to light you to bed, Here comes a chopper to chop off your head!"?
o: Oranges and Lemons (completed by Mr. Charrington just before Winston & Julia's arrest)
e: The traditional rhyme 'Oranges and Lemons' symbolizes lost cultural memory; Mr. Charrington sinisterly completes its final couplet ("Here comes a chopper to chop off your head!") right as the Thought Police raid the upstairs room behind the glass paperweight.

q: In his 1940 essay 'Inside the Whale', Orwell uses Jonah's shelter inside the whale's belly as a metaphor for the quietist, politically detached modernist posture of which American expatriate novelist?
e: In 'Inside the Whale' (1940), Orwell analyzes Henry Miller's 'Tropic of Cancer' (1934) as a passive acceptance of the modern world ("inside the whale"), contrasting it with the committed 1930s Auden-Spender political poets.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of George Orwell's six explicit rules for clear writing at the conclusion of 'Politics and the English Language' (1946)?
o: Never use a metaphor, simile, or other figure of speech which you are used to seeing in print.
Never use the passive where you can use the active.
Never use a long word where a short one will do.
Always prefer foreign phrases and scientific jargon to add scholarly authority.
e: Orwell's 5th rule is the exact opposite of Option D: "Never use a foreign phrase, a scientific word, or a jargon word if you can think of an everyday English equivalent." His 6th rule is: "Break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous."

q: Which 1945 essay by George Orwell — written as a proposed preface to 'Animal Farm' but omitted at publication and only rediscovered in 1971 — denounces voluntary self-censorship by British intellectuals ("Unpopular ideas can be silenced... without the need for any official ban")?
e: 'The Freedom of the Press' (1945, first published in TLS in 1972) was Orwell's suppressed preface to 'Animal Farm', warning against cowardly self-censorship in democratic societies. 'Such, Such Were the Joys' (published posthumously 1952) recalls his grim preparatory school days at St. Cyprian's.

q: In his 1945 essay 'Notes on Nationalism', how does George Orwell crucially distinguish 'Patriotism' from 'Nationalism'?
o: Patriotism is defensive devotion to a particular place and way of life without wishing to force it on others, whereas Nationalism is inseparable from the desire for power and prestige.
Patriotism is aggressive militarism, whereas Nationalism is peaceful cultural love.
Both terms are identical synonyms in Orwell's political vocabulary.
Patriotism applies only to empires, whereas Nationalism applies only to colonies.
e: In 'Notes on Nationalism' (May 1945), Orwell praises Patriotism as defensive and rooted in affection for a place, while condemning Nationalism (which he broadens to include Communism, Trotskyism, and political Catholicism) as power-hungry and indifferent to objective truth.

q: Which famous Cold War term is widely credited to George Orwell, who first used it in his October 1945 'Tribune' essay 'You and the Atom Bomb' to predict a nuclear stalemate between superpowers?
e: In 'You and the Atom Bomb' (19 October 1945), Orwell foresaw a "peace that is no peace" — a permanent "cold war" between two or three monstrous superstates possessing atomic bombs (a vision that also shaped Oceania, Eurasia, and Eastasia in 'Nineteen Eighty-Four').

q: In his celebrated 1940 critical essay 'Charles Dickens', what famous concluding image does Orwell use to summarize Dickens's moral humanism and enduring appeal?
o: "A face that is generously angry — a nineteenth-century liberal, a free intelligence, a type hated with equal hatred by all the smelly little orthodoxies which are now contending for our souls."
"A Victorian reactionary wholly blind to industrial poverty."
"A cold aesthete detached from the common people."
"A revolutionary Marxist ahead of his time."
e: Orwell's 1940 essay 'Charles Dickens' (published in 'Inside the Whale and Other Essays') critiques Dickens's lack of structural economic theory while passionately praising his "generously angry" decency against "all the smelly little orthodoxies."

q: In 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', what is the final chilling sentence of the novel (before the Appendix), signifying the complete psychological annihilation of Winston Smith's individuality?
o: "The clocks were striking thirteen once more."
"He had won the victory over himself. He loved Big Brother."
"We shall meet in the place where there is no darkness."
"Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four."
e: Sitting at the Chestnut Tree Café drinking Victory Gin, hearing news of Oceania's military triumph, Winston gazes up at the giant face of Big Brother and realizes: "He had won the victory over himself. He loved Big Brother." (Note: Winston's diary quote in Ch. 7 is Option D.)

q: In 'Why I Write' (1946), Orwell famously compared ideal, transparent prose style — free from ornament, dishonesty, and ideological fog — to which everyday object?
o: A windowpane ("Good prose is like a windowpane")
e: Orwell concluded 'Why I Write' (1946) with the dictum "Good prose is like a windowpane" — reflecting his lifelong aesthetic commitment to clarity, concrete imagery, and moral honesty, which earned his distinctive critical style the adjective 'Orwellian'.
